front.title: Execution-Time Authority Requirements for AI Agent Actions
front.workgroup: Workload Identity in Multi System Environments

abstract.t: Current work on AI agent identity and authorization establishes which agent is acting and what authority it was granted. It does not establish whether the workload exercising that authority is still in an approved state at the moment it acts, or how much authority a tree of delegated agents has consumed in total. A compromised agent host inherits valid identity, valid credentials, and valid delegations, and every signature it produces verifies.

This document states requirements for binding the authority to take a consequential action to the state of the executing workload at the time of use, for containing consumable authority across a delegation tree, and for recording the result so that it can be evaluated later. It defines no protocol and no wire format. It is offered as input to work on agent identity, agent communication, and transparency records.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The AI Identity Management System draft composes workload identity and OAuth mechanisms for AI agents. It ties credential issuance and renewal to an assessment of workload posture and leaves the evidence format and the verifier to deployments. Credentials are short-lived, but an agent can act many times within one credential lifetime, and the posture that justified issuance is not re-examined at each use.

The architecture proposed for agent communications observes in its security considerations that valid credentials do not establish that a platform is uncompromised. The use cases and requirements draft requires that credential validity be verified at time of use and that revocation propagate through delegation chains, and it places accountability and auditing mechanisms out of scope.

These documents leave the same interval open. Between the moment an authority is granted and the moment it is exercised, four things can change: the software and configuration of the agent, the policy that governs it, the standing of anyone in its delegation lineage, and the amount of authority its siblings and descendants have already used. An attacker who controls the agent host after issuance does not need to forge anything.

This document states requirements that close that interval. They are written so that existing mechanisms can satisfy them: remote attestation , workload identity, OAuth token exchange , and signed transparency statements . The requirements are derived from an open source implementation described in .

section.name: Scope
section.t: In scope: what a decision point needs to know, and to record, before it permits a consequential action by an agent.
Out of scope: agent identifiers and credential formats, discovery, dialog management, policy languages, the behavior of AI models, and any payment protocol. uses a payment as an illustration only.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: An action whose effect persists outside the agent and that the deployment has classified as requiring a decision before execution. Each consequential action has a reversibility class: reversible, reversible with cost, or irreversible.
A statement of authority issued to an agent by a principal or by another agent, in any format.
A root grant together with every grant derived from it by delegation.
Authority expressed as a quantity that use depletes, such as monetary value, request count, records exported, or compute.
The component that permits or refuses a consequential action.
Evidence about the software, configuration, and environment of the workload that will execute the action, in the sense of .
A monotonically increasing value associated with an authority tree. Authority issued under an earlier epoch is not valid.
A named person or organizational role that answers for an agent's consequential actions and can stop them.

section.name: Problem Statement
section.t: A decision to permit a consequential action can be checked at four levels.

dl.dd: Signatures, audiences, expiry, and nonces are valid. Existing mechanisms cover this.
The proposed action falls within a deterministic reading of the grant. Existing mechanisms partly cover this.
The agent, its tools, the decision point, and the credential holder are in an approved state now.

The grant, every grant above it, the posture evidence, and the revocation state are all still valid at the instant of execution, and the authority tree has not already consumed what the action would consume.

section.t: Identity and delegation work addresses the first two. The last two are where a compromised but correctly credentialed agent succeeds. The requirements below address them.

dl.dd: Before permitting a consequential action, the decision point MUST bind together a digest of the exact action, the grant under which it is requested, the revision of the policy applied, a reference to the posture evidence relied on, and the current revocation epoch of the authority tree.
The binding MUST be fixed no later than the decision. A binding assembled afterward from logs does not satisfy this requirement. This matches the decision-time binding requirement in .

The decision point and any key used to exercise the authority MUST NOT be readable or invocable by the AI model whose output proposed the action. This extends the rule in that the model does not hold agent or tool credentials.

For actions in a class the deployment designates, the decision point MUST evaluate posture evidence whose age is within a bound the deployment declares for that class. Evidence gathered at credential issuance satisfies this only if it is within the bound at the time of use.

Posture evidence that is absent or older than the bound MUST be recorded as not established, not as a negative result. The decision point MAY refuse on that basis. This preserves the distinction drawn in .
The bound SHOULD tighten as the reversibility class moves toward irreversible.

section.name: Delegation and Aggregate Containment

dl.dd: A grant derived by delegation MUST NOT exceed the grant it derives from in any dimension, including scope, duration, counterparties, and consumable quantity.

Consumption of consumable authority MUST be counted against the grant used and against every grant above it in the authority tree. A decision point MUST refuse an action that would cause any ancestor's limit to be exceeded.
Where more than one decision point serves an authority tree, they MUST share consumption state or partition the limit among themselves in advance. Independent local counters do not satisfy ETA-8.

section.t: ETA-8 addresses a failure that per-grant limits do not: many descendants each staying within a small limit while the tree as a whole exceeds what the root principal authorized.

dl.dd: Advancing the revocation epoch of a grant MUST invalidate every grant derived from it, without enumerating them.
The decision point MUST compare the epoch bound under ETA-1 with the current epoch at the time of execution, not only at the time of the decision, when the two are separated.

A deployment MUST declare the interval within which an epoch change reaches every decision point for the tree, and MUST treat a decision point that has not confirmed the current epoch within that interval as unable to permit consequential actions. This document sets no numeric value.

An agent permitted to take irreversible actions MUST be associated, in a record the agent cannot modify, with an accountable authority that is able to advance the revocation epoch of the agent's grants without the cooperation of the agent or of any AI model provider.

Where obligations scale with an agent's capability tier, the tier MUST be taken from the registered record and not from a value the agent presents. A missing tier MUST be treated as the most restrictive tier.

Confirmation by the accountable authority, when policy requires it, MUST be bound to the action digest of ETA-1 and obtained over a channel the agent does not control. notes that confirmation during execution needs further design; this requirement states the property that design has to have.

A decision MUST resolve to one of: permit, deny, escalate to the accountable authority, or unresolved. Unresolved applies when the action may have taken effect and its outcome is not known. An unresolved action MUST NOT be resubmitted until it is reconciled.

Every decision, including a denial, MUST produce a signed record containing the binding of ETA-1, the outcome, and for each input whether it was verified by the decision point, asserted by another party, or not established.
The record MUST be verifiable without the cooperation of the agent, the original session, or credentials that were valid at the time, consistent with .

The record SHOULD be expressible as a Signed Statement so that it can be registered with a transparency service. This document does not define a new record format; and the profiles under discussion in the SCITT working group are candidates.

When an action crosses from one protocol or administrative domain to another, the receiving side MUST NOT accept weaker assurance than the grant requires. A grant that requires posture evidence is not satisfied by a bearer token presented on its behalf.

section.name: Relationship to Other Work
section.t: This document adds no mechanism to . It asks that the posture assessment performed at provisioning be available, with a freshness bound, at the point of use, and that authorization tokens be able to carry or reference the items in ETA-1.

ETA-7 restates scope narrowing as required by for multi-hop delegation. ETA-8 and ETA-9 are additional. ETA-16 is compatible with that draft's statement that an operation whose outcome cannot be determined stays unresolved.

defines signed action records, authorities that can stop an agent, and a rule that an edge passes traffic only while it holds current authority state. ETA-12 is satisfied by that rule. This document does not compete with it.
Posture evidence can be conveyed using the architecture in . This document does not profile it.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The requirements assume the decision point is more trustworthy than the agent. If both run in one compromised environment, ETA-3 is not met and nothing here helps. Deployments need to say where the decision point runs and why the agent cannot reach it.

Posture evidence shows that measured software was running. It does not show that the software is free of vulnerabilities, or that an AI model's output is correct or uninfluenced by injected content. An agent in an approved state can still be instructed to take a harmful action that falls within its grant. Aggregate containment limits the damage from that case; it does not prevent it.
A counterparty that is authentic and malicious satisfies every requirement in this document.

Shared consumption state under ETA-9 is a target. An attacker who can reset or partition it defeats ETA-8. An attacker who can delay epoch propagation extends the window in ETA-12; the fail-closed rule in ETA-12 bounds this at the cost of availability, which makes the propagation path a denial-of-service target.

A decision point's signing key can forge records under ETA-17. Registering records with a transparency service limits what a later key compromise can rewrite; it does not help against a key that was compromised when the record was made.
ETA-16 forbids resubmission of unresolved actions because retry after an ambiguous failure is a common way for an irreversible action to be executed twice.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Records under ETA-17 link an action to an agent, a delegation lineage, and an accountable authority. That linkage is the purpose of the record and is also a tracking risk in the sense of .

Records SHOULD carry digests of action parameters and not the parameters. Identifiers for the principal and the accountable authority SHOULD be pairwise or otherwise unlinkable across relying parties, with disclosure to an evaluator on a stated basis. Posture evidence can fingerprint a deployment and SHOULD be referenced by the record and disclosed separately.
Aggregate consumption state reveals the activity of an entire authority tree to whoever holds it. Deployments SHOULD keep that state with the party that issued the root grant.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section is to be removed before publication as an RFC. It follows .

The requirements were derived from the NEXUS reference implementation published by the Cyber Strategy Institute under the Apache 2.0 license . Version 0.6.0 implements the binding of ETA-1, registry-bound capability tiers (ETA-14), monotonic attenuation (ETA-7), aggregate containment (ETA-8), revocation epochs, the four outcomes of ETA-16, and hash-chained decision records with a redacted external form. Each has tests that exercise the refusal path.

Limits of that implementation: posture verification is an interface with a test verifier, not an integration with a hardware root of trust, and stale evidence is refused without being recorded separately as not established (ETA-5). The revocation epoch is kept per principal, which is coarser than the per-grant epoch of ETA-10. Consumption state is a single-host reference store, so ETA-9 is not met across hosts. Records are not yet emitted as SCITT Signed Statements. The implementation has not been independently evaluated and has no production deployment evidence. Its bindings to external payment protocols refuse by default and have not been tested against live counterparties.

section.name: Worked Example: An Irreversible Action
section.t: This appendix is illustrative. A payment is used because it is a familiar irreversible action. The same sequence applies to any action in the irreversible class.
A principal authorizes an agent to spend up to 500 units with a set of merchants over one week. The agent delegates 100 units to each of three sub-agents for separate tasks.

ol.li: A sub-agent proposes a payment of 80 units. The decision point computes the action digest and collects the sub-agent's grant, the policy revision, a reference to posture evidence for the sub-agent's workload, and the tree's revocation epoch (ETA-1).
The posture evidence is 40 seconds old. The deployment's bound for irreversible actions is 60 seconds. The input is established (ETA-4).
The sub-agent has consumed 30 of its 100. The tree has consumed 410 of 500. Permitting 80 would take the tree to 490. Both limits hold (ETA-8).
The decision point permits, signs the record, and releases the action to a credential holder the agent cannot reach (ETA-3, ETA-17).
A second sub-agent then proposes 20 units. It is within its own 100. The tree would reach 510. The decision point denies and records the denial (ETA-8, ETA-17).

The accountable authority learns that the first sub-agent's host was altered and advances the epoch of the root grant. Every derived grant is invalid from that point without being listed (ETA-10, ETA-13).
A payment that was permitted before the epoch change but has not yet executed is checked again at execution and refused (ETA-11).
A payment whose submission timed out is recorded as unresolved and is not retried until its status is reconciled with the payee (ETA-16).

section.t: Step 5 is the case that per-grant limits miss. Steps 6 and 7 are the case that credential expiry alone handles too slowly.
